title: Teaching himself to read and arrange from records and library scores
summary: Gil says he is semi-literate at reading music. He learned arranging by copying records note for note and studying library scores.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: and he's in Germany right now. Doing a concert. In West Germany, a jazz concert in West Germany. He sailed on 22nd October. Yes. But I want to get back to this business of your teaching yourself for a minute.

And we haven't finished talking about your mother, but we started out and let it go and I think I would like to sort of get back to that and then we can get back to the statistics at another point because I think it has a lot to do with how you moved up, let us say, in the music world. And I think that these early origins are as important as anything we can talk about.
So, when you say you taught yourself, how did you actually go about learning how to read music? You had absolutely no, not even in school you had any help, is that it?

I still can't read music too well, you know. I'm like what you call semi-literate in music. And I really never did practice reading music. I can write music for other people, to play you know. But to read other people's music, I'm not too quick at it.
either. That had to have something to do with it. Well my eyesight is, my close-up eyesight is bad. But that really doesn't ......
But do you wear corrective glasses? Oh yes.

I never had the inclination to learn to read very much. Although at one time I had to go to the library all the time to pick the scores out you know, and read them. That's how I learned about orchestration and arranging.
Now that's what I want you to talk about a little bit here. I think that's extremely difficult.

That's the ( ?), library. It's not really hard though. Because I mean, if you know what you want. It's the same thing as going to school to learn it. You simply go and get it and learn it. If you hear it on record and want to know how it's done, if the score is available you go and get it. If the score is not available, then you copy the record yourself. You know, and just play it over and over again until you get every note of it.

That's how I learned really to arrange and how I learned to read really. And to write the notes down was by listening to the record and then painstakingly putting down on paper what I heard on the records, you know.
At first it was slow and after that it gradually (it got to where I?) could do it readily. But that was my first arrangement, I know it was a copy off a record.

As it happens now, the young people they (bottom?) for me to buy the records and listen to them and the next day they've got it down. You know, they finger it instrumentally or in a few days I've got it written down. It's always been like that really.

I mean when you say you're self-taught you really don't mean that you learned all by yourself without any help. I got all the help of everybody I ever heard play. And all the writing I ever wanted to read I got from the library to see how it was done, you know. So I really had to learn from .........
So you would take out books on composition and orchestration and that sort of thing?
